lessons.title: Digester Types: Covered Lagoon, Complete Mix, Plug Flow, Fixed Film
lessons.body:
A digester is just a sealed container where bacteria turn organic waste into biogas. The type you choose depends on your waste, climate, and budget. In Africa, four designs are common.

Covered lagoon: A shallow pond (2-3 m deep) lined with plastic or concrete, covered with a gas-tight cover. Best for very wet waste (less than 3% solids), like pig or dairy flush water. Cheap to build but needs large land area and warm climate (above 20Â°C). Not good for cold nights.

Complete mix: A large tank (often 100-1000 mÂ³) with a mechanical mixer and heating. Handles thick waste (5-10% solids) like food waste or chicken litter. Expensive, needs electricity, but works in any climate. Common on large farms.

Plug flow: A long, narrow trench (10-20 m) covered with a flexible bag. Waste moves slowly from one end to the other. Good for thick waste (10-15% solids) like cattle manure. Simple, low-cost, but needs regular feeding and warm temperatures. Popular in Kenya and Ethiopia.

Fixed film: A tank filled with plastic media or rocks where bacteria grow as a film. Works for dilute waste (0.5-2% solids) and can handle high flow rates. Good for treating wastewater from food processing. Needs careful start-up and consistent temperature.

For a small African farm with 5 cows, a plug flow digester (10 mÂ³) is often best. For a school with kitchen waste, a complete mix (20 mÂ³) may work. Always match the digester to your daily waste volume and solids content. Test your waste: mix 1 liter in a jar, let it settle, and measure the sludge layer. That gives you % solids.

lessons.title: Sizing a Digester: Hydraulic Retention Time and Organic Loading Rate
lessons.body:
Sizing a digester means finding the right volume so bacteria have enough time to eat the waste. Two numbers control this: Hydraulic Retention Time (HRT) and Organic Loading Rate (OLR).

HRT is the number of days the waste stays inside. If you add 100 liters per day and your digester is 2000 liters, HRT = 2000/100 = 20 days. For most African conditions, HRT should be 20-40 days. In cold weather (below 20Â°C), use 40-60 days. In warm climates (25-35Â°C), 20-30 days is fine. Example: A farm with 10 cows produces about 100 kg of manure per day. Mix with equal water to make 200 liters of slurry. For 30-day HRT, digester volume = 200 L/day Ã 30 days = 6000 L (6 mÂ³). Add 20% headspace for gas, so build 7.2 mÂ³.

OLR is how much organic matter (volatile solids, VS) you add per cubic meter of digester per day. Too high, and acids build up; too low, and you get little gas. For plug flow and complete mix, OLR should be 0.5-2.0 kg VS/mÂ³/day. For covered lagoons, 0.1-0.5 kg VS/mÂ³/day. To find VS: take a sample of manure, dry it, and burn it. The weight lost is VS. Cow manure is about 15% VS of total solids. If you have 100 kg fresh manure with 20% solids, that's 20 kg total solids, and 15% of that is VS = 3 kg VS. For a 6 mÂ³ digester, OLR = 3/6 = 0.5 kg VS/mÂ³/day. That's safe.

Always calculate both HRT and OLR. If OLR is too high, increase HRT by making the digester bigger or adding less waste. If HRT is too short, bacteria wash out. Use a simple spreadsheet or the free tool 'Biogas Calculator' from Energypedia.

lessons.title: Mixing in Anaerobic Digesters: Passive and Active Methods
lessons.body:
Mixing keeps bacteria in contact with food, prevents scum layers, and stops temperature pockets. Without mixing, gas production drops by 30-50%. There are two ways: passive and active.

Passive mixing uses the natural movement of gas and liquid. In plug flow digesters, the daily feeding pushes material along. In covered lagoons, gas bubbles rising stir the liquid. You can also install a simple 'gas recirculation' pipe: biogas is drawn from the top and bubbled back through the bottom. This uses no electricity. For a 10 mÂ³ plug flow digester, a 1-inch PVC pipe with a small compressor (12V, 5W) can recirculate gas for 10 minutes every hour. Cost: about $50.

Active mixing uses mechanical or hydraulic energy. Options: (1) Mechanical stirrer: a shaft with blades, powered by a 0.5-2 kW motor. Used in complete mix digesters. (2) Slurry recirculation: a pump moves liquid from the top to the bottom. For a 20 mÂ³ digester, a 0.5 kW pump running 15 minutes every 2 hours works. (3) Bubble mixing: compressed biogas injected at the bottom. Needs a gas compressor.

In Africa, passive mixing is preferred because it's cheap and has no moving parts. For small farms, a simple manual stirrer (a long pole with a paddle) once a day can help. For medium farms (50-200 mÂ³), a solar-powered 12V pump for slurry recirculation costs about $200 and runs 2-3 hours per day. Always avoid over-mixing: it can break up bacterial granules in fixed film digesters. Mix gently for 5-10 minutes per hour. Test your mixing by checking for a uniform color and no floating crust. If you see a thick scum layer, mix more.

lessons.title: Heating Requirements and Insulation for Digesters
lessons.body:
Bacteria work best at 35-40Â°C (mesophilic) or 50-55Â°C (thermophilic). In most of Africa, ambient temperatures are 20-30Â°C, so heating may be needed at night or in highlands. Without heating, gas production can drop by half in cold weather.

First, calculate heat loss. Use this formula: Q = U Ã A Ã ÎT. Q is heat loss in watts. U is insulation value (0.5-2 W/mÂ²Â°C for uninsulated concrete, 0.1-0.3 for insulated). A is surface area of digester. ÎT is difference between digester temperature (35Â°C) and outside air (15Â°C at night). Example: A 10 mÂ³ cylindrical digester (2 m diameter, 3 m tall) has surface area about 25 mÂ². Uninsulated concrete U=1.5. ÎT=20. Q = 1.5 Ã 25 Ã 20 = 750 W. That's like running a 750W heater continuously. Insulate with 5 cm of straw or foam, U drops to 0.3, Q = 0.3 Ã 25 Ã 20 = 150 W. Saves 80% energy.

Heating methods: (1) Solar water heater: circulate hot water through pipes inside the digester. A 2 mÂ² solar collector can provide 500-1000 W in sunny Africa. (2) Electric immersion heater: 1-2 kW, but expensive if grid power is unreliable. (3) Heat from biogas: burn some biogas to heat water. 1 mÂ³ biogas = 6 kWh heat. (4) Compost heat: build a compost pile around the digester. 

Insulation is cheaper than heating. Wrap the digester with locally available materials: rice husks, sawdust, dry grass, or plastic foam. Cover the top with a transparent plastic sheet to trap solar heat. In Kenya, a farmer increased gas production by 40% by building a simple greenhouse over the digester. For a 10 mÂ³ digester, insulation costs about $100 and pays back in 6 months. Always keep the digester temperature stable; fluctuations of more than 5Â°C per day stress bacteria.

lessons.title: Designing Gas Collection and Storage Systems
lessons.body:
Biogas must be collected, cleaned, and stored. A typical system has: gas outlet, pipes, water trap, pressure relief, and storage bag or tank.

Gas outlet: At the top of the digester, install a 1-2 inch PVC pipe. Slope it slightly so condensation drains back. Add a water trap: a T-joint with a vertical pipe that collects water. Empty it weekly. Pressure relief: a simple U-tube filled with water (25 cm deep) that bubbles if pressure exceeds 25 cm water column (about 0.025 bar). This prevents the digester from cracking.

Pipes: Use PVC or HDPE pipes. For a small farm (10 mÂ³ digester), 1-inch pipe is enough. For larger systems, 2-inch. Keep pipe runs short and avoid sharp bends. Bury pipes 30 cm deep if crossing cold areas. Check for leaks with soapy water.

Storage: You need to store gas for cooking when you need it. Options: (1) Floating drum: a inverted steel or plastic drum that rises as gas fills. Simple, but heavy and corrodes. (2) Fixed dome: gas collects in the dome, displacing slurry. Cheap but pressure varies. (3) Bag storage: a low-cost PVC or polyethylene bag (0.5-5 mÂ³). A 2 mÂ³ bag costs $50-100 and holds enough gas for 2-3 hours of cooking. Protect from sunlight and rodents. (4) Gas holder tank: steel tank with a water seal. Expensive but durable.

For most African smallholders, a 2-5 mÂ³ PVC bag storage is best. Connect it after the water trap. Add a valve before the stove. Use a gas pressure gauge (manometer) made from a clear plastic tube with water. Keep pressure between 5-20 cm water column. If pressure is too high, add a second storage bag. Always install a flame arrestor before the stove to prevent fire back into the system. Total cost for collection and storage for a 10 mÂ³ digester: $150-300.

lessons.title: Software Tools for Biogas System Design
lessons.body:
You don't need expensive software. Several free or low-cost tools can help you design a biogas system accurately.

1. Energypedia Biogas Calculator: A free online spreadsheet. Enter your daily waste (kg), solids content (%), and temperature. It gives you digester volume, gas production, and HRT. Works offline if you download it. Used by many NGOs in Africa.

2. BiogasCalc (Android app): Free app for small-scale digesters. You input number of cows, pigs, or people, and it recommends digester size and gas output. Available on Google Play.

3. RETScreen: Free software from Canada. It includes a biogas project model. You can calculate energy savings, costs, and greenhouse gas reductions. Good for writing grant proposals. Runs on Windows.

4. HOMER Energy: Free trial version. Simulates hybrid power systems including biogas generators. Useful for designing a biogas-powered electricity system for a farm or school.

5. Microsoft Excel: You can build your own calculator. Use formulas: Digester volume = daily slurry (L) Ã HRT (days). Gas production = VS (kg) Ã 0.35 mÂ³/kg (for cow manure) Ã 0.8 (efficiency). For example, 10 cows produce 30 kg VS/day. Gas = 30 Ã 0.35 Ã 0.8 = 8.4 mÂ³/day. That's enough for cooking for 4 families.

6. QGIS: Free mapping software. Use it to plan where to place digesters, pipelines, and storage. Useful for community projects.

Start with Energypedia's calculator. It's simple and reliable. Then use Excel to check your numbers. Always validate with real measurements: weigh your waste, test solids, and measure gas with a simple flow meter (a calibrated bag or water displacement). Remember: software is a guide, not a replacement for field experience. Many African biogas projects fail because designers skip basic measurements. Take the time to measure your waste and temperature for one week before designing.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Biogas System Design Fundamentals

This practical reference consolidates the core design decision points for anaerobic digestion (AD) systems in African agribusiness settings. Whether you are sizing a covered lagoon for a 2,000-head piggery in Uganda, specifying a plug-flow digester for a dairy in Kenya, or evaluating a fixed-film reactor for agro-processing wastewater in Nigeria, the fundamentals below determine whether your biogas investment delivers reliable gas, manageable maintenance, and a defensible return on capital.

The lessons in this module cover six areas: digester types (covered lagoon, complete mix, plug flow, fixed film), sizing (hydraulic retention time and organic loading rate), mixing (passive and active), heating and insulation, gas collection and storage, and software design tools. This reference distills those into a working checklist, two data tables, a safety warning, and curated further reading.

Digester Type Selection at a Glance

Selection hinges on feedstock total solids (TS), flow rate, climate, and capital available. Covered lagoons suit dilute, high-volume manure slurries in warm climates. Complete mix reactors handle high-strength, variable feedstocks but need mixing energy. Plug flow works for thick dairy manure. Fixed film suits soluble, low-solids industrial waste with short HRT.

Table 1. Digester type selection matrix for African agribusiness contexts
Digester Type Typical TS (%) HRT (days) Climate Fit Best African Use Case
Covered Lagoon 0.5â3 20â60 Warm, tropical Piggery and dairy flush-water systems
Complete Mix 3â10 15â30 Any (heated) Mixed manure, food and agro-processing waste
Plug Flow 11â14 15â25 Moderate to warm Dairy and cattle manure with bedding
Fixed Film <2 (soluble) 1â5 Any (heated) Palm oil mill effluent, food processing wastewater

Source: Adapted from FAO (2011) Manual on Biogas Technology; IRENA (2018) Biogas for Domestic Cooking; and US EPA AgSTAR Anaerobic Digester Project Development Handbook (2018).

Sizing: HRT and OLR

Hydraulic retention time (HRT) is the average time feedstock remains in the digester. Organic loading rate (OLR) is the mass of volatile solids (VS) fed per unit reactor volume per day. Both must be satisfied simultaneously. If HRT is too short, methanogens wash out. If OLR is too high, volatile fatty acids (VFAs) accumulate and the process acidifies.

HRT (days) = Digester working volume (mÂ³) Ã· Daily feed volume (mÂ³/day)

OLR (kg VS/mÂ³Â·day) = Daily VS fed (kg/day) Ã· Digester working volume (mÂ³)

For a Ugandan piggery producing 8 mÂ³/day of slurry at 3% TS with 80% VS, daily VS load is 8 Ã 0.03 Ã 0.80 Ã 1000 = 192 kg VS/day. At an OLR of 2.0 kg VS/mÂ³Â·day, working volume = 96 mÂ³. At an HRT of 30 days, working volume = 240 mÂ³. The larger figure governs â design for 240 mÂ³, giving an actual OLR of 0.8 kg VS/mÂ³Â·day, which is conservative and stable.

Table 2. Design parameters and typical values for mesophilic anaerobic digestion
Parameter Typical Range Comment
HRT â covered lagoon 20â60 days Longer in cooler highland areas
HRT â complete mix 15â30 days Heated to 35 Â°C
OLR â mesophilic 1.5â4.0 kg VS/mÂ³Â·day Start low, ramp up over 4â8 weeks
Temperature 30â38 Â°C (mesophilic) Biogas yield peaks near 35 Â°C
pH 6.8â7.4 Below 6.6 signals acidification
Biogas yield (manure) 0.3â0.5 mÂ³/kg VS Methane 55â70%
C/N ratio 20â30:1 Co-digest to balance

Source: FAO (2011) Manual on Biogas Technology; US EPA AgSTAR (2018); and IRENA (2018).

Mixing, Heating, and Gas Collection

Mixing. Passive mixing uses gas bubbles, thermal gradients, and influent flow. Active mixing uses mechanical stirrers, pumped recirculation, or biogas recirculation. Active mixing improves mass transfer and prevents crusting but consumes 5â15% of gross biogas output. For small African farms, passive mixing plus periodic manual agitation is often the pragmatic choice.

Heating and insulation. Mesophilic digestion at 35 Â°C is 2â3Ã faster than ambient in cool highland regions. Heat demand = (feed mass Ã specific heat Ã temperature rise) + digester heat losses. Insulate with straw bales, earth berms, or rigid foam. Solar water heating can offset 30â60% of heating load in sunny regions.

Gas collection and storage. Design collection pipes with a slight slope to condensate traps. Use HDPE or PVC with gas-tight joints. Storage options include low-pressure flexible bags (0.5â5 kPa), floating drum covers, and medium-pressure steel vessels. Size storage for 4â12 hours of peak demand. Include a flare for surplus gas and a pressure relief valve.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Biogas is Flammable and Asphyxiating

Biogas contains 50â70% methane and is explosive at 5â15% concentration in air. Hydrogen sulphide (HâS) is toxic at concentrations above 10 ppm and lethal above 300 ppm. Carbon dioxide displaces oxygen in confined spaces.

  • Never enter a digester, storage tank, or pit without forced ventilation, a calibrated multi-gas monitor, and a standby observer.
  • Install flame arrestors on all gas lines and a pressure/vacuum relief valve on the digester cover.
  • Locate flares away from buildings, livestock, and public roads â minimum 15 m separation.
  • Use only explosion-proof electrical fittings within 5 m of gas equipment.
  • Train all operators on HâS detection and emergency shutdown procedures.

Software Tools for Design

Several free or low-cost tools support sizing and financial modelling:

  • US EPA AgSTAR Co-Digestion Economic Analysis Tool (CoEAT) â feedstock blending and economics.
  • Anaerobic Digestion Model No. 1 (ADM1) â open-source kinetic model for advanced simulation.
  • RETScreen Clean Energy Management Software â financial and GHG analysis for biogas projects.
  • HOMER Energy â hybrid renewable and biogas system optimisation.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Confirm feedstock volume and TS/VS â sample for at least 7 days before sizing.
  2. Calculate both HRT and OLR â design to the larger required volume.
  3. Match digester type to TS and climate â use Table 1 as a screening tool.
  4. Provide a minimum 20% volume buffer for sludge accumulation and storm inflow.
  5. Specify mixing method and energy budget â cap active mixing at 10% of gross gas.
  6. Insulate and, where feasible, heat to 35 Â°C â model heat demand before committing.
  7. Size gas storage for 6â12 hours of peak demand â include flare and relief valve.
  8. Run a financial model (CoEAT or RETScreen) before capital approval.

Further Reading

  • FAO â Manual on Biogas Technology (2011)
  • IRENA â Biogas for Domestic Cooking (2018)
  • US EPA AgSTAR â Anaerobic Digestion Resources
  • US DOE â Anaerobic Digestion Basics
  • NREL â Anaerobic Digestion Model No. 1 (ADM1) Documentation

Prepared for RISE AFRICA Skills â Biogas Systems Module. Business-first guidance for African agribusiness operators, developers, and financiers.

quiz.q: Which digester type is best for very wet waste with less than 3% solids?
quiz.explanation: Covered lagoons are designed for dilute waste like flush water from pig or dairy operations.

quiz.q: What is the typical hydraulic retention time (HRT) for a biogas digester in a warm African climate?
quiz.explanation: Warm temperatures (25-35Â°C) allow faster bacterial action, so 20-30 days is sufficient.

quiz.q: If you add 200 liters of slurry per day and want a 30-day HRT, what digester volume do you need?
quiz.explanation: Volume = daily slurry Ã HRT = 200 L/day Ã 30 days = 6000 L.

quiz.q: What does OLR stand for in digester sizing?
quiz.explanation: OLR is the amount of volatile solids fed per cubic meter of digester per day.

quiz.q: For a plug flow digester, what is a safe organic loading rate (OLR)?
quiz.explanation: Plug flow and complete mix digesters typically handle 0.5-2.0 kg VS/mÂ³/day.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of passive mixing?
options: C) It works in all climates
quiz.explanation: Passive mixing uses natural gas movement or manual effort, so no electricity is needed.

quiz.q: Which mixing method uses a pump to move liquid from top to bottom?
quiz.explanation: Slurry recirculation pumps liquid from the top back to the bottom of the digester.

quiz.q: How often should you mix a small farm digester with a manual stirrer?
quiz.explanation: Daily manual stirring helps prevent scum and keeps bacteria in contact with food.

quiz.q: What is the optimal temperature range for mesophilic bacteria in a digester?
quiz.explanation: Mesophilic bacteria thrive at 35-40Â°C, which is common in many biogas systems.

quiz.q: What is the formula for heat loss from a digester?
options: A) Q = U Ã A Ã ÎT
B) Q = m Ã c Ã ÎT
quiz.explanation: Heat loss (Q) equals overall heat transfer coefficient (U) times surface area (A) times temperature difference (ÎT).

quiz.q: If U=1.5, A=25 mÂ², and ÎT=20Â°C, what is the heat loss?
Which insulation material is locally available in many African farms?
quiz.explanation: Rice husks, sawdust, and dry grass are common, low-cost insulation materials.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a water trap in a biogas gas collection system?
options: A) To add moisture to the gas
quiz.explanation: A water trap collects water that condenses in the gas pipe, preventing blockages.

quiz.q: What is the typical pressure relief setting for a small biogas digester?
quiz.explanation: A 25 cm water column (about 0.025 bar) is a common safe pressure limit.

quiz.q: Which gas storage option is a low-cost PVC bag?
quiz.explanation: PVC or polyethylene bags are cheap, light, and easy to install for small-scale storage.

quiz.q: What should you install before a biogas stove to prevent fire back?
quiz.explanation: A flame arrestor stops a flame from traveling back into the gas line.

quiz.q: Which free software tool is recommended for biogas system design and includes a project model?
quiz.explanation: RETScreen is a free tool from Canada that includes biogas project analysis.

quiz.q: What does the Energypedia Biogas Calculator require as input?
options: A) Daily waste, solids content, temperature
quiz.explanation: The calculator uses waste amount, solids percentage, and temperature to estimate digester size and gas output.

quiz.q: In Excel, what formula gives gas production from volatile solids (VS)?
quiz.explanation: For cow manure, gas yield is about 0.35 mÂ³/kg VS, and efficiency is about 0.8.

quiz.q: If 10 cows produce 30 kg VS/day, what is the estimated gas production?
Which digester type uses a long, narrow trench covered with a flexible bag?
quiz.explanation: Plug flow digesters are long trenches where waste moves slowly from one end to the other.

quiz.q: What is the typical solids content for waste fed to a complete mix digester?
quiz.explanation: Complete mix digesters handle thick waste with 5-10% total solids.

quiz.q: What is the main disadvantage of a covered lagoon in cold climates?
options: B) It needs large land area
D) It cannot handle wet waste
quiz.explanation: Covered lagoons require large land area and work poorly in cold temperatures.

quiz.q: Which mixing method is best for a fixed film digester?
quiz.explanation: Fixed film digesters need gentle mixing to avoid breaking up bacterial granules.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of adding 20% headspace in digester sizing?
quiz.explanation: Headspace allows gas to accumulate above the slurry without pushing out liquid.

quiz.q: Which of these is a passive mixing method?
quiz.explanation: Gas recirculation uses rising biogas bubbles to mix the digester without electricity.

quiz.q: What is the heat loss from an uninsulated concrete digester with U=1.5, A=25 mÂ², ÎT=20Â°C?
Which software is free and useful for mapping biogas project locations?
quiz.explanation: QGIS is a free, open-source mapping tool for planning pipelines and digester placement.

quiz.q: What is the recommended pressure range for a biogas system using a manometer?
quiz.explanation: Most small biogas appliances work best at 5-20 cm water column pressure.

quiz.q: What should you do if your digester's OLR is too high?
options: B) Increase HRT by making digester bigger
quiz.explanation: Increasing HRT (by enlarging the digester or reducing feed) lowers OLR and prevents acid buildup.
